outcome: Nothing has settled, or moved any quantity the bullet asks about, since 26 January 2024: the conjecture is still open on every primary and reference source I opened, and the only in-window items are a Lean formalisation of amicable/sociable-cycle definitions (arXiv, 12 January 2026), a 2025 preprint on a different Collatz-type divisor-sum map, and two expository pieces from 2024.
problem_asks: Read from the bullet alone: (1) For every positive integer n, the aliquot sequence n, s(n), s(s(n)), … with s(m) = σ(m) − m (the sum of the proper divisors of m) is not infinite and non-repeating. (2) Because s is a deterministic map, an infinite sequence with bounded terms must eventually repeat; so part (1) is equivalent to: every aliquot sequence is bounded. The bullet's 'infinite but non-repeating' and the Wikipedia/literature 'bounded' formulations therefore describe the same question. (3) The claim is universal over all starting integers and names no particular starting value (276 appears in the literature as the smallest unresolved case, not in the bullet). The bullet does NOT ask: (a) that every sequence terminates, or ends at a prime, a perfect number, or a sociable cycle (Wikipedia's lead states this fuller Catalan–Dickson form, which the bullet does not carry); (b) which cycles occur; (c) density, averages or typical behaviour, which is the Guy–Selfridge counter-conjecture's territory and is not named in the bullet; (d) any quantitative growth bound.

events.what_happened: Hendrik W. Lenstra Jr. showed that there are aliquot sequences of arbitrary prescribed length that increase at every step. The proof is recorded in Stan Devitt's 1976 Calgary MSc thesis (supervised by Richard Guy), as reported in a search summary of the Bosma survey and ProofWiki. I did not open the thesis or a Lenstra write-up.
events.revisions: None found. Lenstra's own earlier write-up, if any, was not located, so 1976 is an upper bound on the first written argument.
events.delivers: Finite monotone increasing runs of any prescribed length. It produces no infinite increasing sequence, so it does not show any orbit is unbounded.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: no infinite orbit is exhibited and no boundedness claim is proved.
events.time_since_posted: About 50 years; a search summary says later surveys (Bosma; Pomerance's notes) cite it, but I did not open those.
events.direction: Gives the Guy–Selfridge side a finite-length foothold only. It does not cut either way on whether an infinite orbit can be unbounded.
events.object: Aliquot sequences of arbitrary prescribed length, each strictly increasing, built recursively from prime powers using Euler's totient (per the ProofWiki summary, which I did not open). Finite runs, not infinite ones.

events.what_happened: Benito, Creyaufmüller, Varona and Zimmermann, 'Aliquot Sequence 3630 Ends After Reaching 100 Digits', Experimental Mathematics 11(2) (2002) 201–206. The sequence from 3630 is run to termination at 1, after its terms reach 100 digits. A search summary also reports the Lehmer-five sequences computed to at least 112 digits. I did not open the paper; the bibliographic details come from the Wikipedia article's citations.
events.delivers: One starting value (3630) observed to terminate at 1, plus a record for digit length. Each finite termination is one more instance of the terminating branch of Catalan's claim. Under the bullet's universal wording, that moves nothing.

checked_by.who: Experimental Mathematics (journal of record); referees not named in sources I saw
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the computational note

events.directly_checkable: The 3630 trajectory can be recomputed from σ(n) − n with factorisation of each term; the paper's 100-digit terms require large-number factorisation.
events.direction: Discounted: a termination observed for one starting value is consistent with the conjecture and bears on no universal claim.

events.what_happened: Paul Zimmermann's aliquot records page logs two dated entries on the 276 trajectory. On 11 September 2009, factors he found for sequences 276, 552, 564, 660, 966 and others were added to Markus Tervooren's Factoring Database, thanks to Karsten Bonath. On 25 March 2017 he stopped extending the 276 sequence at index 2051, after finding no ECM factor of a 201-digit cofactor (tested to 60 digits). A search summary also cites Brent's champions list crediting Ryan Propper with splitting a c199 from the 276 sequence at index 2063 using GMP-ECM 6.4.4; that entry is undated and I did not open it.
events.revisions: Page last dated entry 25 March 2017. No later dated entry is on the page.
events.delivers: Factorisation support and a computed index for one starting value (276): trajectory computed to index 2051 by March 2017. This is a single case; it does not settle whether the 276 orbit is bounded or terminates, and the bullet is a universal claim.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, including the fate of the 276 orbit, which the page leaves open.
events.time_since_posted: Last entry about 9.5 years before this record.
events.directly_checkable: Each term is σ(m) − m of the previous term; the ECM non-factorisation claim at index 2051 can be re-run with GMP-ECM.
events.doubts: The 2017 stop means the index-2051 cofactor remained unfactored after ECM to 60 digits. Later indices (see the OEIS event) imply further computation not dated on Zimmermann's page; who did it is not established here.
events.direction: Neutral on the statement. It records how far one orbit has been followed.
events.object: The aliquot trajectory of 276, computed to index 2051 (cofactor 201 digits) when Zimmermann stopped in 2017.
people: Ryan Propper (c199 split, undated, per search summary)

events.what_happened: Wieb Bosma and Ben Kane, 'The aliquot constant', arXiv:0912.3660 (submitted 18 December 2009; Quarterly Journal of Mathematics 63 (2012) 309–323 per a search summary). They show the geometric mean of s(n)/n over even n exists and is below 1 (µ ≤ 0.969…, equivalently the constant λ is negative). The abstract reads this as probabilistic evidence that aliquot sequences tend to stay bounded.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 only (18 Dec 2009). The arXiv page lists no journal reference; the QJM 2012 citation comes from a search summary.
events.delivers: An averaged statement: the geometric mean over even n of the one-step growth factor s(n)/n is below 1. This is a statement about an average over n, not about any single orbit, so it does not establish boundedness of any orbit. The bullet's universal claim remains open.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: boundedness of every orbit is not established.

checked_by.who: Quarterly Journal of Mathematics (journal of record), per search summary
checked_by.where: https://arxiv.org/abs/0912.3660 (journal details from search summary, not opened)

events.time_since_posted: Published 2012; reproved and sharpened by Pomerance in 2018 (see that event).
events.doubts: The arithmetic mean of s(n)/n over even n is above 1 (about 1.056 per the Guy–Selfridge heuristic), so averaging heuristics point both ways. Bosma and Kane themselves note that an average above 1 does not by itself settle boundedness, comparing an alternating ×5, ×1/5 sequence, which stays bounded despite its average growth factor exceeding 1.
events.direction: Evidence toward boundedness on average. It cuts toward the conjecture in heuristic terms and does not decide any orbit.

events.what_happened: Wieb Bosma, 'Aliquot sequences with small starting values', arXiv:1604.03004 (submitted 11 April 2016). All aliquot sequences with starting values below one million are computed until each terminates (at 1 or in a cycle) or reaches an entry of 100 decimal digits. Dependencies and statistics are recorded.
events.delivers: A census over starting values below 10^6. It is finitely many instances of a universal claim and moves nothing the bullet asks. Sequences that reach the 100-digit cutoff are left unclassified, so this does not show that any orbit is bounded.
events.time_since_posted: About 10.5 years; no separate engagement with the census found in my searches.
events.directly_checkable: Each reported sequence can be recomputed from σ(n) − n; the 100-digit cutoffs need large-number factorisation.
events.doubts: The census stops at a 100-digit cutoff, so the sequences that reach it are not classified, and the abstract does not say whether any of them is unbounded.
events.direction: Finite computational evidence, consistent with the conjecture on the sequences classified. It moves no universal quantity.

events.what_happened: Kevin Chum, Richard K. Guy, Michael J. Jacobson Jr. and Anton S. Mosunov, 'Numerical and statistical analysis of aliquot sequences'. The journal version is in Experimental Mathematics 29(4) (2020) 414–425; the arXiv comment says the accepted manuscript was published by Taylor & Francis on 18 June 2018 (DOI 10.1080/10586458.2018.1477077); arXiv:2110.14136 was posted 27 October 2021. The paper computes the geometric mean of s_k(n)/s_{k−1}(n) for n ≤ 2^37 and k ≤ 10, extends untouchable-number computations to 2^40, and estimates aliquot growth with a Markov-chain model built on thousands of sequences. Talk abstracts from 2016 (Mosunov, CNT) previewed similar figures; I treat them as preview, not write-up.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 27 Oct 2021 only. The journal publication date (18 June 2018, per the arXiv comment) precedes the arXiv posting. I date the event to the earlier written version. Either date is before the window, so this does not change the in-window count.
events.delivers: Computational and statistical evidence on the average growth of iterates, including geometric-mean figures for s^k with k ≤ 10 and a Markov-chain estimate. It does not prove that any orbit is bounded or unbounded, and the averaged quantities are not the per-orbit question in the bullet.

checked_by.who: Experimental Mathematics editors and referees (Taylor & Francis)
checked_by.qualification: Peer review by a specialist computational number-theory journal
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper for publication (2018 accepted manuscript; 2020 issue)

events.time_since_posted: Published 2018/2020; arXiv 2021. OEIS A008892 cites it.
events.doubts: The authors describe their own results as evidence for and against the Guy–Selfridge heuristic. Per the 2016 talk abstract summary, the geometric means of s^k(2n)/s^(k−1)(2n) exceed 1 for X = 237 and k = 6–10, but decline as X grows for fixed k. That pattern is the reason the authors read it both ways.
events.direction: Heuristic and statistical evidence, read both ways by the authors. It cuts neither way on the bullet's universal claim.

events.what_happened: Carl Pomerance, 'The aliquot constant, after Bosma and Kane', Quarterly Journal of Mathematics 69(3) (2018) 915–930, DOI 10.1093/qmath/hay005. It reproves the Bosma–Kane asymptotic with a stronger, power-saving error term, and treats the geometric mean of s(s(2n))/s(2n) alongside s(2n)/(2n); a search summary of Mosunov's abstract reports that these means agree for n > 1. I did not open the paper; Pomerance's Dartmouth PDF notes were not extractable.
events.delivers: Asymptotics for geometric means over n of iterates; no statement about any single orbit. It moves the averaged growth quantity and leaves the per-orbit bullet untouched.

checked_by.who: Quarterly Journal of Mathematics (Oxford University Press), editors and referees
checked_by.where: https://doi.org/10.1093/qmath/hay005 (not opened; cited from OEIS and search summary)

events.direction: Average-growth asymptotic, consistent with the heuristic evidence for boundedness. It does not decide any orbit.

events.what_happened: OEIS A008892 (the aliquot sequence starting at 276) carries a note by N. J. A. Sloane dated 11 January 2023: 'The trajectory has been calculated to 2145 terms, and is still growing, term 2145 being a 214-digit number.' The b-file (Tyler Busby) lists terms 0–2157, with terms 0–2127 from Daniel Suteu and 2128–2140 from Jeppe Stig Nielsen. The same entry states it is an open question whether the sequence ever reaches 0.
events.revisions: OEIS page last modified 11 October 2026 (per the page), but the page does not say what changed. The term-count note is dated 11 Jan 2023.
events.delivers: A computed trajectory of one starting value to about 2145–2157 terms. It establishes nothing about whether the 276 orbit is bounded; the entry itself says the question is open. A single case of a universal claim moves nothing the bullet asks.
events.directly_checkable: Terms are σ(m) − m of the previous term, so the trajectory can be recomputed; the 214-digit terms need factoring (FactorDB).
events.doubts: The source of the 2145-term computation and its date are not given on the page; I could not reach FactorDB to check the current index.
events.direction: Neutral on the statement: finite data on one orbit.
events.object: The aliquot trajectory of 276, computed to 2145 (up to 2157 in the b-file) terms; term 2145 has 214 digits.

events.what_happened: Agbolade Patrick Akande, 'The number of preimages of iterates of ϕ and σ', arXiv:2401.04073 (submitted 8 January 2024). It gives upper bounds on the number of preimages of iterates of Euler's totient ϕ and of σ, extending Erdős–Pomerance bounds.
events.delivers: Counting preimages of σ-iterates. It does not address the growth or boundedness of orbits of s(n) = σ(n) − n, which is what the bullet asks. A neighbouring question on the same function.
events.direction: None on the bullet. It is about a different question, preimage counts.

events.what_happened: Numberphile video 'An amazing thing about 276', presented by Ben Sparks, on the aliquot sequences and the open status of 276. The video page's description says only that the video 'discusses aliquot sequences and why 276 holds a surprise'. Wikipedia's article on 276 cites it with date 2024-03-06. The Numberphile page itself shows 'May 1' with no year, so the year is not confirmed by the video page.
events.delivers: Nothing new: an expository video about an open problem with no new claim or computation in its description.

events.what_happened: Andrew Chambers, 'Aliquot sequence: An unsolved problem', IB Maths Resources blog (Intermathematics), 17 May 2024. Introduces the aliquot sequence and the Catalan–Dickson conjecture, runs small examples, and gives a Python snippet. It states that 276 is the smallest number whose sequence is unknown, that a laptop run of about 30 minutes produced 44 terms for 276, and that the code 'might be enough to disprove a conjecture' if run long enough on a supercomputer.
events.delivers: Nothing new. The post makes no new mathematical claim; its remarks about disproof are speculative and it says so only in general terms.
events.time_since_posted: About 29 months; no published comment or follow-up found in searches.

events.what_happened: Ritesh Dwivedi and Rohit Yadav, 'A Divisor-Sum Analogue of the Collatz Map', arXiv:2506.01830 (v1 submitted 2 June 2025). The map studied is R(n) = σ(n) for odd n and n/2 for even n, which the paper explicitly says is not the aliquot map n ↦ σ(n) − n. It conjectures every orbit reaches 1 (which would imply there is no odd 2^k-perfect number) and proves a pointwise descent estimate for the induced map on odd integers, which the authors state does not iterate.
events.revisions: v2 3 Jun 2025 (title shortened, per the page comment); v3 14 Sep 2026 described as substantially revised.
events.delivers: Nothing on s(n) = σ(n) − n. The paper concerns a different Collatz-type map, and the authors contrast it with the aliquot case. It is a cognate question about a divisor-sum iteration, not the bullet.
events.time_since_posted: About 16 months from v1; no engagement found in my searches.
events.doubts: The paper's own proved estimate does not iterate, which the authors state. I found no later assessment.
events.direction: Different map. It does not cut either way on the bullet.

events.what_happened: Zhipeng Chen, Haolun Tang and Jingyi Zhan, 'Formalization of Amicable Numbers Theory', arXiv:2601.07444 (cs.LO, submitted 12 January 2026). A Lean 4 formalisation of amicable-number theory: it defines the proper divisor sum, sociable cycles, and betrothed numbers, and verifies Thābit's formula and rules, the Borho–Hoffmann method, and computational search bounds. The paper reports 2076 lines, 139 theorems and zero sorry placeholders in its conclusion. It verifies Poulet's length-5 sociable cycle (12496, 14288, 15472, 14536, 14264) computationally.
events.delivers: Machine-checked definitions of sociable cycles and computational verification of specific cycles and amicable pairs. It contains no general theorem about iterates of s, so it does not establish boundedness, termination or any cycle classification for aliquot sequences.
events.time_since_posted: About 9 months; no public engagement found in my searches.

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 (the paper describes its formalisation as built on Lean 4 and Mathlib)

events.directly_checkable: The five-term sociable cycle can be checked by hand: each term is σ(m) − m of the previous term and the cycle closes after five steps.
events.doubts: The sorry-free status is the authors' own statement in the conclusion. I did not compile the repository, and I did not verify the Mathlib dependency claim beyond the paper's text.
events.direction: Neutral on the conjecture. It formalises definitions and specific instances, not the general claim.
events.object: The length-5 sociable cycle 12496 → 14288 → 15472 → 14536 → 14264 → 12496 under s(n) = σ(n) − n, verified computationally and formalised in Lean (per the paper). It is an explicit finite object, not a counterexample to anything.

disputes.summary: Sources differ on Dickson's 1913 change. Pomerance's slides describe it as the boundedness claim 'Every orbit is bounded'. ProofWiki's historical note describes it as allowing that a sequence may end in a sociable chain. Wikipedia's lead gives the fuller form (ends in a prime, a perfect number, or a sociable cycle). The bullet asks only the non-repeating part, which is the boundedness formulation. This is a framing difference, not a priority dispute, and I have not picked a winner.

summary: Result: no in-window event moved any quantity the bullet asks about. The conjecture (no aliquot sequence is infinite and non-repeating, equivalently all orbits of s(n) = σ(n) − n are bounded) is still listed as open. Primary and reference sources I opened agree on this: Wikipedia's article (the Catalan–Dickson conjecture 'remains open'; 276 is the smallest unresolved case); OEIS A115350 ('So far 276 is the smallest number for which the termination of the aliquot sequence is not known') and A008892 (the 276 trajectory computed to 2145 terms, dated 11 Jan 2023; 'It is an open question whether this sequence ever reaches 0'); Zimmermann's records page (last dated entry 25 March 2017, when the 276 sequence was stopped at index 2051); Yamasaki's page (© 2017; 'It is unknown whether there exists any integer n such that the aliquot sequence is not bounded'; smallest unknown 276); MathWorld (page updated 2 Oct 2026; 'The conjecture remains open to this day'); and the OEIS wiki (no revision dates; 'neither conjecture is resolved'). The pre-window literature is averaged and computational: Bosma–Kane (2009, QJM 2012) show the geometric mean of s(n)/n over even n is below 1, which is heuristic evidence for boundedness; Bosma's 2016 census covers starting values below 10^6 with a 100-digit cutoff; Chum–Guy–Jacobson–Mosunov (Experimental Mathematics, 2018 accepted, 2020 issue; arXiv 2021) gives statistics that the authors read both ways; Pomerance (QJM 2018) reproves Bosma–Kane. None of these shows any single orbit bounded or unbounded. Lenstra's theorem gives arbitrarily long finite increasing runs only. Nothing in the sources reports an unbounded or infinite non-repeating aliquot orbit, and the Guy–Selfridge counter-conjecture is still unrefuted and unproven. In-window (since 26 Jan 2024) I found: an expository blog post (17 May 2024) and a Numberphile video (2024, date conflicting) with no new claim; a 2025 preprint on a different Collatz-type divisor-sum map R(n) = σ(n) for odd n, n/2 for even n (arXiv:2506.01830, v1 2 June 2025; the paper explicitly says this is not the aliquot map); and a Lean 4 formalisation of amicable-number theory including sociable-cycle definitions and the computational check of Poulet's length-5 cycle (arXiv:2601.07444, 12 Jan 2026; no general theorem about aliquot iteration). Close calls: (i) whether the averaged results (Bosma–Kane, Chum et al., Pomerance) count as 'a quantity named in the statement' moving. The statement is about each orbit, and averages over n are not that quantity, so I record them as evidence, not as partial resolution. (ii) Whether the 2025 Collatz-type paper is a 'changed version' of the question: it is a different map, so I record it as discounted. (iii) Whether the Numberphile video is an event at all: I record it as expository with no claim. AI involvement: no AI system is named for this problem in any source I read. I read the full HTML text of the two in-window papers, and neither mentions AI, LLMs, or an AI-assisted tool; the 2026 Lean paper's only funding acknowledgement is a Shanghai grant. The pre-window papers name no AI because they predate the systems in question; for the Chum et al. 2021 arXiv PDF I read only the abstract and could not extract the full PDF text. I also checked the 2026 AI-batch sources for aliquot content: the openai/math repository (719 manuscripts in 372 families, per its landing page; the press reports 722) lists no aliquot, divisor-sum, Dickson or Guy–Selfridge item in the full catalogue I read in six chunks; the 2026 preprint 'GPT, the Counterexample Machine' (arXiv:2608.29595) has no aliquot content in its full text. Erdős-problem AI results and AlphaProof Nexus news concern other problems. The Erdős problems database entry for untouchable/non-cototient (#418, last updated 8 Dec 2025) does not mention aliquot iteration. No AI-assisted result on this problem was found, and no claim to one was found.
competing_reading: The strongest case for a different reading: the averaged growth results (Bosma–Kane 2009/2012, Pomerance 2018, Chum et al. 2018–2021) are the main quantitative progress on the conjecture's heuristics, and the arithmetic/geometric-mean argument is a route by which 'almost all' orbits might be shown bounded. A reader who takes boundedness in probability to be the operative quantity could count Pomerance's equal-means asymptotic as a partial move. Against this: the bullet quantifies over every starting integer, so an average over n, however sharp, leaves the universal claim open, and the authors themselves present the data as evidence for and against the Guy–Selfridge heuristic.
what_would_settle_it: A proof that every orbit of s(n) = σ(n) − n is bounded (which would settle the bullet on the boundedness side), or an exhibited orbit with s^k(n) → ∞ or a non-repeating infinite trajectory (which would refute it). Short of that, the in-window status is settled by the absence of any such result in the arXiv math.NT listing and in OEIS, FactorDB and Zimmermann's pages for 2024–2026. Clarifying the open dates would require: the Numberphile upload date (2024-03-06 per Wikipedia versus 'May 1' with no year on the video page); the date and origin of the OEIS A008892 term count (page modified 11 Oct 2026, change not stated); and the full Chum et al. 2021 PDF to confirm the AI-free statement.
